title: Notes on San Marino
author: yorwba
tldr: San Marino has stayed independent for at least 700 years. It survived by being too small, pious and loyal for any neighbor to bother conquering. In the 20th century it copied its neighbors with mild fascist and communist governments. Today it is a quiet, rural country that barely uses its sovereignty for tax tricks.

keyPoints: San Marino has 33,500 people and covers about 61 square kilometers. Its official founding date of 301 AD is doubtful. The first evidence of an independent government is a land deed from 1243.

The author counts 13 attempts to absorb San Marino between about 1300 and 1862. Each time it survived through diplomacy, protectors or luck. Its main asset was that conquering a poor, pious village looked bad and gained little.
San Marino changed its image to suit each stronger neighbor. It was Catholic for the popes and republican for Napoleon. It was traditional for the Congress of Vienna and fascist under Mussolini.

In 1797 San Marino refused Napoleon's offer of land reaching the Adriatic. Its leaders believed that staying small kept it safe. Garibaldi, who sheltered there in 1849, probably helped it stay independent after Italian unification.

Communists and socialists won the 1945 election. When Italy stopped its annual customs payment, they opened a casino in 1949. Italian police then searched every car at the border, and the casino closed in 1951.

The author found the countryside hard to walk and never met a Sammarinese local. Most workers the author met were Italian, Moldovan or Brazilian. In 2020 the four Sammarinese banks reported 63% of their loans as non-performing.
article.whyItMatters: Read the original for the full list of 13 near-annexations and the 1957 standoff between two rival governments. It also has the photos, the travel notes on museums and gun shops, and the tax comparison with Italy.

comments.overview: A small, friendly thread. Readers praised the writing and the author's survival story. The longest exchange left San Marino behind and argued whether parliamentary republics stay stable better than presidential ones.

themes.title: Is boring government the goal?
themes.synthesis: One commenter took the article's line about nothing happening since World War II as proof that boring is good. A Polish commenter argued that parliamentary republics with weak, indirectly elected presidents rarely turn authoritarian. Others pushed back. They said the key is a president with no executive power, and they listed parliamentary republics that did fall to dictators.

quotes.author: epolanski
quotes.text: I don't think any modern country should aim at anything less than boring, albeit unstable, parliamentary republics

quotes.author: roryirvine
quotes.text: I think it's the explicit lack of executive power that's the important part, not the lack of a direct popular vote.

themes.title: Switzerland and the cuckoo clock
themes.synthesis: A commenter quoted Harry Lime's line from The Third Man that Swiss peace produced only the cuckoo clock. Replies listed Swiss pharma and finance and noted that cuckoo clocks came from Germany. Others said Switzerland had a short civil war in 1847. They added that quiet countries depend on calm neighbors, so bigger states cannot simply copy them.

quotes.author: p-e-w
quotes.text: Things would be very different in Switzerland if it bordered the Eastern Bloc or the Mediterranean Sea.

quotes.author: xhevahir
quotes.text: The kind of boredom enjoyed in San Marino and Liechtenstein is probably not available to bigger countries.

themes.title: What counts as a country
themes.synthesis: The top thread said the idea of a country with fixed borders is modern. Medieval loyalty ran through personal ties, so the claim of the oldest continuous republic is hard to judge. Replies split country, state and nation-state apart and pointed to Scotland and Aruba as odd cases. One commenter said the Peace of Westphalia changed diplomacy but did not invent countries.

quotes.author: jcranmer
quotes.text: This is what makes adjudicating the "oldest continuous republic" hard, because at what point do we say that the homages San Marino is paying stops counting as being part of that country?

quotes.author: quink
quotes.text: It’s a big deal but to claim that countries weren’t a thing before it is a bit of an overstatement.

themes.title: Tax havens
themes.synthesis: One commenter said microstates exist only for tax avoidance and gave Andorra as the example. Another replied that the article found San Marino does little of this. A Rimini local added that San Marino did have that reputation until about 15 years ago.

quotes.author: holoduke
quotes.text: The only reason why these states exist is because of tax evasion methods used by business people in countries around them.

quotes.author: canjobear
quotes.text: Did you read the article? San Marino doesn’t do much of this.

themes.title: The writing and the region
themes.synthesis: Many readers called the piece long but hard to put down, and some wanted a book of the author's travel notes. Readers enjoyed how mild San Marino's political swings were. Locals and visitors defended Rimini against the word rundown. A Rimini resident said its disco clubs closed as tourism shifted to families and older couples.

quotes.author: ykl
quotes.text: they did a mini version of everything else that was going on the world in the 20th century, but it turns out that when you're a small peaceful moderate country, it's hard for things to get too too out of hand at any given moment.

quotes.author: mdrzn
quotes.text: in the last 20 years we progressively lost all of the disco clubs that we had between Rimini and Riccione, because of the change in tourism (now it's mainly families or old couples, less and less youngsters).

comments.consensus: The article is thorough and enjoyable. San Marino's calm depends on its size and its peaceful neighbors.
comments.dissent: Some readers saw microstates as tax shelters or retirement communities rather than real countries. Others rejected the claim that parliamentary systems resist authoritarian rule.

contrarian.author: mdrzn
contrarian.text: Maybe not now (and not in the last 15 years or so), but San Marino was VERY well known for being a "cash" place where money was passed around and you could do "nero" (avoid taxes, avoid invoices, etc).
contrarian.why: It adds a local's memory that off-the-books cash deals were common knowledge, which the article's search of formal studies could not show.
